title: Nvidia CEO Admits Affair With Suspected Chinese Spy
dek: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits an affair with a woman US intelligence believes is a Chinese spy — an executive at a Megaspeed, a Singaporean cloud provider and major Nvidia customer. Because Nvidia anchors the AI build-out and Jensen has been the industry's strongest advocate for normalized AI trade with China, this is a geopolitical and market story. Plus: Anthropic heads to roadshow at a shrinking valuation, OpenAI's round closes light, and the labs hint at a scientific-discovery phase transition.

oneIdea.headline: Jensen's affair isn't a tabloid story — it's a China policy story.
oneIdea.summary: If this were only about Jensen Huang's personal failings, the show would stay away. But Nvidia is the biggest company in the world and the anchor of the AI build-out, and Jensen has been Washington's most effective voice against a total ban on chip exports to China. An affair with a suspected MSS agent who works at a customer accused of funneling compute to Chinese labs puts every one of his China decisions under question. Congress is circling, Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation, and some argue the leaks themselves are a strategic move to put Nvidia on a national-security leash. The markets are buying the dip for now. The bigger risk is to the dovish case on China and AI.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Little clinical relevance, but a supply-chain point
items.body: This is a story about one company's chief executive and American export policy, and nothing in it changes clinical practice. The practical link is that almost every AI tool the NHS buys runs on Nvidia hardware. NLW sees a policy risk; Zitron alleges a revenue and legal one. Either would reach us only indirectly, through price or availability of cloud services.

items.title: Conflicts of interest are judged by appearance
items.body: The sharpest point made is that intent is beside the question: once a personal relationship overlaps a commercial one, every decision is suspect. The same standard applies to us in procurement. Anyone advising a practice, PCN or ICB on an AI supplier should declare ties early, however innocent.

items.title: Key-person risk in suppliers
items.body: Markets are asking whether one man is replaceable. Smaller health technology suppliers often depend on a founder or one clinical lead. It is reasonable to ask a scribe vendor who holds clinical safety responsibility, and what happens to the service if that person leaves.

the_other_side.text: Zitron, writing a day later, argues the affair distracts from the real story, which he says is revenue: that Nvidia has inflated its sales through intermediaries passing restricted chips to China, a matter reported in detail for over a year and largely ignored. He cites a short seller's allegation, which he says he trusts, that about a fifth of Nvidia's last fiscal-year revenue came from China, and press reports that Nvidia's general counsel contacted officials about a Commerce Department probe of Megaspeed. He calls for Huang and the general counsel to go, and says Megaspeed is "the tip of the iceberg", quoting the short seller's source. These are his allegations; Nvidia denies wrongdoing.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is how much of Nvidia's business, and its China advocacy, rests on chips reaching China through intermediaries. Both accept as fact that Huang admitted the affair, that Megaspeed was a large customer already under Commerce Department scrutiny, and that the board has opened an inquiry. The empirical question is the size of the diverted sales; the observable is what the board, Congress and the Justice Department find, and whether Nvidia restates or loses revenue booked through South-East Asia. The residue is worldview: whether this is one man's lapse inside a sound company, or typical of an industry that bends rules for growth. For Whittemore to be vindicated, the inquiries must find no compromise and the damage must fall on China policy, not the accounts. For Zitron, investigators must show material illicit revenue and bring charges. Both are polemicists with incentives: Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both think the dovish case on chip exports is badly damaged. Watch Huang's closed-door session with Congress later this month.

headlines.headline: Anthropic heads to roadshow as its valuation keeps sliding
headlines.summary: Investor talk of a $2 trillion valuation has fallen to $1.5–1.6T, and Bloomberg reports some institutional buyers now want $1.1T, close to the $965B Anthropic raised at in May. Anthropic is reportedly starting its roadshow this week, aiming to list before Thanksgiving and still targeting $80B at $1.5T, per the FT.

headlines.headline: Is this the boom's first real correction?
headlines.summary: Open-model researcher Nathan Lambert says that if tech keeps sliding on the Jensen news, this could be remembered as the first major correction: debt went too far, then the election and Jensen hit in quick succession, with Anthropic possibly IPOing at the bottom. Andrew Curran's other view is that believers can now get in at about half price.

headlines.headline: A lower Anthropic price is good news for retail
headlines.summary: NLW doubts the IPO lands all the way at $1.1T. But retail investors are providing a lot of exit liquidity for early investors who had access to Anthropic deals, so the lower the valuation, the better for them.

headlines.headline: OpenAI's round closes well short of target
headlines.summary: OpenAI closed $11B at a $1.25T valuation, down from a $30B, $1.4T target in September. It will keep raising at that valuation toward $20B, working with banks to reach high-net-worth individuals and retail investors.

headlines.headline: SoftBank goes from $60B to hundreds of millions
headlines.summary: SoftBank put $60B into OpenAI's past two rounds but only hundreds of millions this time, a defensive move as its stock sits 60% below its June high. A mystery seller dumping $500M of data center debt turned out to be ING, not SoftBank. Elon Musk added to the confusion by claiming SoftBank is "defaulting on their turbine orders."

headlines.headline: OpenAI sends its CFO to shore up the narrative
headlines.summary: On CNBC, Sarah Friar said "a good CFO always raises money when she can," cited 70% Q3 business growth with enterprise revenue doubling, and argued "the demand for AI is real" and that anyone disputing it is making "a losing argument."

headlines.headline: Microsoft lets an aging Oracle compute deal lapse
headlines.summary: Microsoft declined to renew a 2023 GPU rental arrangement with Oracle that was an early sign of the ChatGPT-era chip crunch. Sources say the aging chips, reportedly A100s three generations old, no longer suited its needs.

headlines.headline: First real evidence of old chips aging out
headlines.summary: The headlines overstate it, but NLW notes this may be the first real evidence of older chips reaching the end of their depreciation cycle. That has been a key bear case from people like Michael Burry, so investors will pay attention.

headlines.headline: Powered, current-gen data centers are the real prize
headlines.summary: Microsoft, the most conservative hyperscaler, exited a UK data center deal with Nscale over power delays and is reportedly rethinking all its neocloud agreements. There is no clear evidence this reflects weaker AI demand. Instead, data centers with power connections and the latest GPUs are worth far more than ones still under construction or only promised.

headlines.headline: Google buys out Crusoe's troubled Wyoming project
headlines.summary: The unfinished site, announced with plans to scale to 10 gigawatts, struggled with energy and construction delays, rising costs, and a lack of tenants. Google had reportedly pressured Crusoe to leave since the summer, and now plans to invest $17B in it. It shows how hyperscalers can benefit when neoclouds wobble.

headlines.headline: We are witnessing a genuine phase transition in the pace of scientific discovery.
headlines.attribution: Pushmeet Kohli, VP at Google DeepMind
headlines.summary: Kohli promised a glimpse in releases over the next few weeks. Meta's Tom Mann and OpenAI's Greg Brockman echoed him, with Brockman saying frontier models with lots of test-time compute are "becoming the engine of scientific discovery."

headlines.headline: Speculation grows that the labs have autonomous research
headlines.summary: Aggregator Andrew Curran thinks all three big labs have internal models that choose their own research directions, with results arriving this month. Riley Brown says it feels like nothing has happened since Opus 5.5, "but that is about to change."

headlines.headline: Why the show is covering a sex scandal
headlines.summary: If this were only about Jensen's moral failings, the show would steer clear. But Nvidia is the biggest company in the world, Jensen has been tech's strongest advocate for normalized AI trade with China, and the story carries major geopolitical and market implications.

headlines.headline: Who Alice Huang is, and why Megaspeed matters
headlines.summary: Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) is an executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean cloud provider and large Nvidia customer. Megaspeed gave Chinese AI labs remote access to export-banned Nvidia GPUs, which China hawks have called a loophole for over a year. US officials also suspect it smuggled chips, though that is unproven.

headlines.headline: A White House memo flagged her as an MSS spy last spring
headlines.summary: The New York Times reports a classified memo, drafted under Marco Rubio's oversight, identified Alice as a spy for China's Ministry of State Security and called the relationship romantic. It was circulated ahead of Trump's May trip to Beijing. The FT says officials were privately frustrated with Jensen, who was almost left off that trip.

headlines.headline: I was unfaithful to my wife. There is no excuse for what I did.
headlines.attribution: Jensen Huang, in a company-wide email
headlines.summary: Jensen's Sunday-night company-wide email was a lengthy apology to his family, employees, board, and partners. It did not address the geopolitical side of the scandal.

headlines.headline: Nvidia's board opens an independent investigation but backs Jensen
headlines.summary: Assisted by outside counsel, the board cast Jensen as the target of a foreign intelligence effort. It says it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but will examine all available information, while expressing confidence in Jensen and the leadership team. China's foreign ministry calls the spy allegations "groundless speculation and slander."

headlines.headline: Defenders say no bad intent; critics say intent isn't the issue
headlines.summary: Shaun Maguire and Bill Ackman defended Jensen as a great but human founder, irreplaceable for America's AI leadership. Critics answered that nobody gets seduced by a spy intending to harm national security. The real problem is that every China decision Jensen made is now suspect, and if removing him upends US AI policy, that is a key-man risk problem.

headlines.headline: The core question is the conflict of interest, not secrets
headlines.summary: Commentators like Ryan Fedasiuk and Dmitri Alperovitch argue the bigger issue is whether the relationship shaped decisions to export to Megaspeed and defend it, even after Commerce began investigating it for diverting chips to China. Others suggest she may not have been after state secrets at all, just restricted GPUs.

headlines.headline: Is the leak itself a move in the chip war?
headlines.summary: Taiwanese analyst Andrew Lu argues the scandal's purpose is to discredit Jensen's lobbying against sanctions, reverse H200 export approvals to China, and put Nvidia on a national-security leash. Under the third goal, three congressional committees now examine its security, and an independent board probe effectively plants a Washington watchdog inside Nvidia.

headlines.headline: Commerce approved H200 buyers that may not exist
headlines.summary: The Times reports Commerce approved dozens of Chinese companies to handle H200s, some tied to sanctioned firms or military contractors. One, New Matrix, lists a Beijing headquarters with no light fixtures, let alone desks. Days earlier, Nvidia began requiring Southeast Asian data centers to enroll in its GPU-tracking fleet intelligence system.

headlines.headline: I haven't heard he's done anything wrong.
headlines.summary: Trump says Jensen should remain CEO and that he would happily bring him on his Asia trip later this month, while admitting "you never know what is going on." Whether that position holds as the story evolves is an open question.

headlines.headline: Congress is coming from both sides
headlines.summary: Senator Chris Coons, incoming chair of Senate Foreign Relations, promised investigations into what he called an administration that "isn't corrupt"-free. Before the story broke, the Republican chairs of House Foreign Affairs, the China Select Committee, and Intelligence had already summoned Jensen to a closed-door meeting later in November.

headlines.headline: Markets flinch, then buy the Nvidia dip
headlines.summary: S&P futures shed around $300B when they opened Sunday night and erased the loss within about five minutes, a $650B swing the Kobeissi Letter called the strangest record in stock market history. Monday, Nvidia fell as much as 8.8% before buyers clawed back roughly half the dollar loss, with little spillover into broader tech so far.

headlines.headline: How indispensable is Jensen Huang?
headlines.summary: Investor Jim Osman asks how markets price a CEO they can no longer fully trust. Dan Ives says Jensen "is not replaceable, and that is worry for The Street." Others aren't so sure, and DealBook made the question its headline.

headlines.headline: Three things to watch from here
headlines.summary: Setting aside the personal elements, NLW points to three things: the market implications, further investigations by Nvidia or the US government, and whether Jensen and Nvidia can still argue for more dovish policy on China and AI.
